idiom_name: defer the release at the acquisition point (defer f.Close(), optionally merging the teardown error into a named result)
implementation_notes: defer is Go's replacement for the destructor: the deferred call runs when the enclosing function returns - on a normal return, during a panic, and when runtime.Goexit unwinds a goroutine - with deferred calls running LIFO, so acquire/defer-release pairs release in reverse order. The owner object disappears: the pairing is written at the acquisition site and the body stays ordinary code, which suffices because nothing can leave the function without the deferred call running. Release is function-scoped rather than block- or object-scoped, so a loop that acquires per iteration needs its body moved into a helper, and lifetimes that cannot be expressed as a defer (caches, shared pools, resources released by another goroutine) use explicit ownership or runtime.AddCleanup (Go 1.24) instead.
pitfalls: A defer inside a loop defers until the function returns, so a loop that opens one resource per iteration accumulates open handles; wrap the per-iteration body in a function (or a func literal called immediately) so each iteration releases before the next.

defer f.Close() evaluates the receiver at defer time while defer func() { f.Close() }() reads f when it runs: reassigning the resource variable between the two makes the closure close the wrong handle (or panic on nil).

The deferred call has no error channel: a close failure that only matters when the body succeeded is either merged into a named result or silently dropped, and a deferred Close on a nil receiver panics.
